doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Why live and club recordings differ and getting Les McCann to love the studio
summary: Dorn says a good live record captures a moment. He fixed Les McCann's dislike of the studio with a second tape machine so the tape never stopped.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I think some artists may play a little different because they’re thinking this could be heard a lot. Someone could be listening to this.

The second you say we’re recording live — I made a lot of live records, most of them were not successful. When I say not successful, they didn’t become gigantic live recordings you know. Like Cannonball at the Jazz Workshop or Horace at the Village Gate or you know, Ramsey at the Bohemian Caverns, but when you get a live record that works, it works because you can’t get that in a studio. It only happens with the audience and the room and the weather and the night and whatever it is all kind of line up in the crosshairs for a moment. The tapes that I have and the tapes that I like to put out capture people doing what they did day in and day out. You know I was in the clubs for six or seven years in Philly. I saw everybody who was working the circuit. And one of the things that used to confuse me was why do they sound so incredible in the club and then their records, while good, don’t have that same feeling. So for instance I saw Les McCann at the Showboat a bunch of times. We kind of became friends when I was on the radio. And his records were okay, but in the club he was unbelievable. So when we signed him to Atlantic, you know, I wanted to find out why do you sound one way in a club and another way in the studio. He said, “I hate the studio.” He said, “it’s always somebody staring at you saying ‘take one’ ‘we ran out of tape,’” whatever it is. I said no problem. I said I can fix that. And I could. So what I did was I brought a second tape machine in so we never had to stop the tape, we had a half hour’s worth of tape. And I said, “just play, do what you want, forget we’re making a record.” Now you can’t completely forget you’re making a record, but if you get out of the way the, “okay take three, uh we’re out of tape.” You know, just let the musician do what he does. And if he’s got something that he does that works and he’s comfortable, you’ll eventually get it. So Les went from hating the studio to falling in love with the studio, and then we made lots of great records because we had a way of capturing what it is that he did. That’s important.
